series_items.subject: [PATCH 1/2] mm/mempolicy: use vm_normal_folio_pmd() in queue_folios_pmd()
series_items.patch_summary: This patch series addresses a bug in the mm/mempolicy code, specifically in the queue_folios_pmd function. The issue arises when dealing with VM_PFNMAP regions and huge zero PMDs, causing the folio to land in unpopulated vmemmap and leading to incorrect behavior. The patch uses vm_normal_folio_pmd() instead of pmd_folio(), which correctly handles these cases and prevents the bug.

patches_submitted.patch_summary: This patch series addresses an issue where special page table walkers (pmd_folio()) are called on PMDs that do not map refcounted struct pages, leading to faults when accessing folio fields. The patches modify the pmd_folio() calls in two walkers and introduce a new function vm_normal_folio() for PMD halves, matching the existing PTE halves. This change affects four callers of vmf_insert_pfn_pmd(), which installs special PMDs holding raw pfn mappings without memmap entries. As a result, mbind(MPOL_MF_STRICT) over PMD mapped VM_PFNMAP regions now returns 0 instead of -EIO.

patches_reviewed.subject: Re: memcg stats flushing (WAS "Re: [PATCH] fuse: disable default bdi strictlimiting")
patches_reviewed.patch_summary: This patch aims to improve performance by reducing unnecessary flushing of memory cgroup (memcg) statistics. It introduces a new approach that allows memcg stats to be flushed only when the number of updates exceeds a certain threshold, rather than at regular intervals. This reduces the overhead of flushing and improves performance, especially for deeper memcg depths. The patch also explores alternative approaches, such as scaling the flush threshold based on the memcg limit, but concludes that the new approach is more effective.

review_comments.author: Yosry Ahmed
review_comments.summary:
Reviewer Yosry Ahmed expressed surprise at the performance difference between rstat and other stats flushing methods at high memcg depths (8-32 levels), questioning whether this is a significant issue given other operations' costs, and wondering if the constant cost of rstat updates would dominate in practice.

Reviewer noted that rstat's iteration of all child cgroups could potentially be optimized by taking advantage of cache locality, as multiple contiguous stats may be stored in the same cacheline.

Reviewer Yosry Ahmed suggested analyzing the effect of update latency on various update paths, specifically pointing out that zswap_store() is not significantly affected and suggesting to investigate other hot update paths, likely in networking.

Reviewer Yosry Ahmed suggested that the analysis should be extended to include the update paths and determine whether the additional cost of rstat has a significant impact on performance.

Reviewer Yosry Ahmed expressed concern that the patch may not be suitable for vmscan and zswap paths, suggesting that the flush cost is acceptable in other areas but may not be feasible in these specific cases.
sentiment_signals: concern about applicability to vmscan and zswap
review_comments.raw_body:
There goes my dream if an rstat-free world :')

I am very surprised though that you care about hierarchies this deep.
I don't think we have anything close to even 8 at Google, and in all
my previous testing I usually test up to 4 or 5 levels. I suspect at
that level the difference might be acceptable. But aren't other
operations also really expensive at that depth? I imagine the charging
path is really slow if it has to do atomic updates for 32 parents. Is
the update path really a problem given everything else?

Given the constant cost of rstat updates, it also seems like
memcg_vmstats_needs_flush() is mostly evaluating to true and skipping
the parent walk. I wonder how much this remains true in practice, I
think Shakeel mentioned that it does help in production.

---

I think that's only part of the story. rstat iterates all children
cgroups as well. I think reading multiple contiguous stats may
actually be really cheap since they are likely in the same cacheline.

---

Hmm interesting analysis, but I actually think a more interesting one
is the effect of the update latency in respective update paths. For
example, in the zswap_store() case you analyzed earlier, it ends up
being in the noise. I would check what the hottest update paths are
(probably networking?) and check what the update paths are, to check
if they are really sensitive to the increased update cost. It could be
the case that at least stats that are used by in-kernel flushers do
not really care about the extra update cost.

---

Yup, this is exactly what I mean. This is a good analysis for the cost
of the flush: how much it matters end-to-end. Even though the full
flush is 14x more expensive according to your numbers, it seems like
it ultimately doesn't affect performance much. I would do the same for
the update paths, see if the extra cost really matters. WDYT?

---

If we can eat the cost of the flush here that's great, but I think we
can't say the same for the vmscan and zswap paths (at least)? :/

review_comments.author: Joanne Koong (author)
review_comments.summary:
The author agrees that the performance issue arises from the writeback path and explains that there is only one stat update charge per folio lifecycle.

The author acknowledges a potential issue in the writeback path, where the threshold of 64 * nr_cpus can be quickly exceeded by sustained writes, affecting performance for order-0 folios.

The author acknowledges that the flush cost measured in the benchmark may be due to rstat locking, but expresses uncertainty about its contribution.

The author acknowledges the extra overhead of rstat on updates, particularly in the lru path where it holds the lru lock, which is already a contention point. They express concern that moving all callers off rstat would make the walk more expensive due to per-cpu counters spilling onto multiple cachelines.

The author acknowledges that the extra overhead of rstat is not always necessary and agrees to remove the rate-limiting based on time instead of stats updates, but notes that lock contention remains an issue.

Author Joanne Koong is addressing concerns about the performance of rstat in comparison to other methods, specifically (a) and (b), on high memcg depths. She acknowledges that the logic in vmscan seems weird and plans to investigate further, but does not address the specific performance issue with (a) and (b). She also expresses uncertainty about whether exactness is necessary for zswap and suggests using the non-ratelimited version of rstat if an error tolerance is acceptable.
review_comments.raw_body:
I agree. This aligns with what I saw when running the page counter
approach for zwap on depth 32. For the writeback path though, the
dirtying / writeback folio lifecycle is just stat updates. There's a
charge, but that happens only once, when the folio enters the page
cache.

---

I think for the writeback path, this is probably often encountered in
practice, since the threshold is 64 * nr_cpus and any sustained write
would cross that quickly. It would matter most with order-0 folios
since there's 4 updates incurred per folio independent of folio size.

---

In that benchmark, the flush cost was measured at the leaf of the
memcg chain, so I don't think there were any children to iterate here.
Maybe some of it is attributed to the rstat locking? I'm not too sure.

---

Extrapolating a bit from the synthetic benchmarks, at depth 8, I think
the extra overhead incurred on an update comes out to roughly around
25ns, and at depth 16, around 48ns. I haven't looked at the networking
path, but the lru path (__update_lru_size()) looks concerning, as it
would have that extra overhead while holding the lru lock, which "is
already a heavy contention point on memory-heavy workloads" [1]. As I
understand it, reclaim, compaction, and the page cache path all
serialize on that lock.

If we were to move all the callers off rstat, I think this also would
unfortunately make the walk more expensive. As I understand it, each
stat would be a per-cpu counter which would be added to the
memcg_vmstats_percpu struct, and that would have to spill onto
multiple cachelines. Or maybe I'm missing something here and there
would be a better way to do it.

---

imo ideally it would be great to minimize any overhead we can where if
we don't need the precision for a certain stat, then it would be
preferable to not incur any extra overhead for it on updates if the
overhead saved on reads doesn't justify it. In the grand scheme of
things though, I think in most cases, the extra overhead/latency isn't
really discernible except at high depths and except for the lock
contention issue mentioned above.

I don't really have an issue with rstat for cases like writeback where
we're not doing a lot of reads compared to updates, but I think we do
need to get rid of the rstat rate-limiting, as it seems so arbitrary
to rely on two seconds for stats being updated. Bounding it by time
and not stats_updates feels wrong. Even in the cases where precision
doesn't matter, it seems better to give those callers a higher stats
updates threshold depending on how much error they can tolerate, than
to rely on a blanket 2 seconds.

---

I haven't tried out the vmscan repro or run any benchmarks on that
path, but the logic in vmscan seems weird to me, as it will always
conclude that there were no refaults whenever reclaim scans faster
than the refaults counter advances (which I think would be most of the
time under memory pressure). I'm thinking maybe we could do something
similar to what Usama did in [1] where we fold the refault delta into
a per-lruvec accumulator and let it decay. I'm planning to look more
into this and will follow up then.

For the zswap path, it's still a bit unclear to me whether exactness
is necessary or whether the 64 * nr_cpus error tolerance is
acceptable. If that error tolerance is acceptable, I think it makes
sense to use the non-ratelimited version of rstat with no forced
flushing, given that reads are supposed to be rare since rarely
anybody (from what I understand) in practice sets zswap.max. Quick
benchmarks at depth=4 with zswap.max set at every level, 20 workers on
80 cpus:  rstat forced = ~7,600 stores/s, rstat unforced = ~300k
stores/s, and hierarchical per-cpu counters = ~440k stores/s. The
hierarchical per-cpu counters outperforms rstat unforced on the stores
given that it removes the flush, but we already see massive
improvements from using rstat unforced over rstat forced.

Thanks,
Joanne

[1] https://lore.kernel.org/linux-mm/20260727162550.2032-4-usama.arif@linux.dev/

patches_reviewed.subject: Re: [RFC PATCH] mm/mglru: fix ineffective memory protection for non-kswapd reclaim
patches_reviewed.patch_summary: A patch to fix ineffective memory protection for non-kswapd reclaim in the mm/mglru module, proposed as an RFC PATCH.

review_comments.author: Johannes Weiner
review_comments.summary: Requested the addition of a #ifdef CONFIG_LRU_GEN block to ensure the fix is only applied when LRU generation is enabled.

review_comments.author: Ridong Chen
review_comments.summary: Confirmed the fix and agreed to add it, but no further details were provided.
review_comments.raw_body:
On 8/28/2026 1:21 AM, Johannes Weiner wrote:
> On Wed, Aug 26, 2026 at 09:30:54PM +0800, Ridong Chen wrote:
>> From: Ridong Chen <chenridong@xiaomi.com>
>>
>> memory.min/low is silently bypassed for MGLRU during global proactive
>> reclaim (writing to the root memory.reclaim) and global direct reclaim.
>> It can be reproduced as follows:
>>
>>    # echo 7 > /sys/kernel/mm/lru_gen/enabled
>>    # cd /sys/fs/cgroup
>>    # mkdir -p a/b
>>    # echo 100M > a/memory.min
>>    # echo +memory > a/cgroup.subtree_control
>>    # echo 100M > a/b/memory.min
>>    # echo $$ > a/b/cgroup.procs
>>    # dd if=/dev/zero of=/tmp/testfile bs=1M count=200
>>    # cat a/b/memory.current
>>    222650368
>>    # echo 500M > memory.reclaim
>>    -bash: echo: write error: Resource temporarily unavailable
>>    # cat a/b/memory.current
>>    6070272
>>
>> memory.min is 100M, yet reclaim drops a/b down to 6M, breaking the
>> protection.  The traditional LRU path is not affected because
>> shrink_node() calls mem_cgroup_calculate_protection() for each memcg it
>> visits during a top-down tree walk.
>>
>> Commit 30d77b7eef01 ("mm/mglru: fix ineffective protection calculation")
>> moved the protection computation into lru_gen_age_node(), which only
>> runs for kswapd.  Non-kswapd global reclaim reaches shrink_one() through
>> lru_gen_shrink_node() -> shrink_many() without any protection
>> computation, so emin/elow remain stale or zero.
>>
>> Introduce mem_cgroup_protection_path() which computes emin/elow along
>> the root-to-target path only by iterating through the cgroup ancestors
>> array top-down.  This avoids the full tree traversal that would be
>> needed with mem_cgroup_calculate_protection(), limiting the cost to
>> O(depth) per memcg - typically 3-5 levels.
> 
> Right, because of the memcg-lru...
> 

Yep, that's it.

>> --- a/mm/memcontrol.c
>> +++ b/mm/memcontrol.c
>> @@ -5198,6 +5198,48 @@ void mem_cgroup_calculate_protection(struct mem_cgroup *root,
>>   	page_counter_calculate_protection(&root->memory, &memcg->memory, recursive_protection);
>>   }
>>   
>> +/**
>> + * mem_cgroup_protection_path - compute protection along root->memcg path
>> + * @root: the top ancestor of the sub-tree being checked (NULL for root_mem_cgroup)
>> + * @memcg: the target memory cgroup
>> + *
>> + * Walk the ancestor path from @root down to @memcg and compute the effective
>> + * protection at each level.  This is safe for isolated queries because it
>> + * ensures parents are computed before children.
>> + */
>> +void mem_cgroup_protection_path(struct mem_cgroup *root,
>> +				struct mem_cgroup *memcg)
>> +{
>> +	bool recursive_protection =
>> +		cgrp_dfl_root.flags & CGRP_ROOT_MEMORY_RECURSIVE_PROT;
>> +	struct cgroup *cg;
>> +	int root_level, i;
>> +
>> +	if (mem_cgroup_disabled())
>> +		return;
>> +
>> +	if (!root)
>> +		root = root_mem_cgroup;
>> +
>> +	if (memcg == root)
>> +		return;
>> +
>> +	root_level = root->css.cgroup->level;
>> +	cg = memcg->css.cgroup;
>> +
>> +	rcu_read_lock();
>> +	for (i = root_level + 1; i <= cg->level; i++) {
>> +		struct mem_cgroup *cur;
>> +
>> +		cur = mem_cgroup_from_css(cgroup_css(cg->ancestors[i],
>> +						    &memory_cgrp_subsys));
>> +		if (cur)
>> +			page_counter_calculate_protection(&root->memory,
>> +					&cur->memory, recursive_protection);
>> +	}
>> +	rcu_read_unlock();
>> +}
> 
> Please wrap this in a #ifdef CONFIG_LRU_GEN block.

Will add.

-- 
Best regards
Ridong

series_items.subject: [PATCH 1/5] mm/huge_memory: do not touch frozen folios in deferred_split_isolate()
series_items.patch_summary: This patch modifies the deferred_split_isolate() function in the Linux kernel's huge_memory module to avoid touching folios that are frozen by calling folio_ref_freeze(). The current implementation treats a zero refcount as an indication that the folio is going away, but this can lead to unnecessary unqueuing of folios. The patch introduces a check for the folio being under folio_ref_freeze() and skips it instead of trying to isolate it. This change ensures that the owner of the frozen folio is responsible for its fate and prevents unnecessary unqueuing.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v4 01/11] mm, swap: add virtual swap device infrastructure
series_items.patch_summary: This patch introduces the virtual swap device infrastructure, which allows for dynamic allocation of swap space and enables features like zswap and zero-filled pages without a physical swap device. The virtual swap device is created when the 'vswap' kernel parameter is set to 'on', and it lives for the lifetime of the kernel. The patch also includes changes to various files such as mm/swap.h, mm/page_io.c, and mm/vswap.h to support this new infrastructure. The dynamic-cluster allocator is wired in, but no allocation path can select it yet, with subsequent patches expected to add the necessary paths.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v4 02/11] mm, swap: support zswap and zero-filled swap pages as vswap backends
series_items.patch_summary: This patch adds support for zswap and zero-filled swap pages as virtual swap (vswap) backends, allowing compressed or zero-filled pages to be stored without pre-allocating physical swap slots. The vswap layer decouples PTE swap entries from physical backing, enabling efficient compression and detection of zero-filled pages. However, this patch only supports zswap and zero-page backends, with physical disk backing and real writeback to be implemented in later patches. Additionally, THP (Transparent Huge Pages) swapin is disabled for vswap entries until further development.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v4 03/11] mm, swap: prepare the swap IO path for vswap
series_items.patch_summary: This patch prepares the Linux kernel's swap IO path to support virtual swap (vswap) by allowing it to submit IO for a swap entry other than folio->swap. The current implementation derives the target device and sector from folio->swap, which is not suitable for vswap entries backed by physical slots. To address this, the patch introduces a new field in the swap_iocb structure to store the sector of the swap entry, and updates various functions to use this new field instead of folio->swap. This change enables the batching path to serve both vswap entries and physical entries mapped directly into PTEs without any functional changes.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v4 04/11] mm, swap: support physical swap as a vswap backend
series_items.patch_summary: This patch adds support for physical swap as a backend for the virtual swap layer, allowing zswap to decline pages and allocate physical slots on demand. The physical slot is tracked via a pointer-tagged swap_table entry, and readahead scans are modified to skip these entries. The patch also includes changes to handle failed reads of vswap entries and to bypass vswap when zswap is disabled at the host level or for the folio's cgroup.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v4 05/11] mm, swap: enable THP swapin for vswap entries
series_items.patch_summary: This patch enables the swapping in of large anonymous memory pages (THP) for vswap entries when they share a contiguous run of physical swap slots on a synchronous IO device. This allows for more efficient swapping and reduces the number of faults that occur during the process. The patch also introduces checks to ensure that zswap-backed or mixed-backing batches are not swapped in as THPs, and that fault retries occur at smaller orders when necessary.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v4 06/11] mm, swap: write back vswap zswap entries to physical swap
series_items.patch_summary: This patch adds support for writing back zswap-backed vswap entries to physical swap. It mirrors the existing zswap writeback path, but allocates physical backing on demand at writeback time instead of pre-allocating it. The zswap shrinker no longer skips vswap entries unless there is not enough physical swap space available. This allows for more efficient use of swap space and improves system performance.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v4 07/11] mm, swap: reclaim physical slots backing cache-only vswap entries
series_items.patch_summary: This patch reclaims physical slots backing cache-only vswap entries when the swap is more than half used. Cache-only vswap entries are those where the vswap entry's swap_count has dropped to 0, but its folio is still in the swap cache. The patch introduces a new flag, SWP_RMAP_CACHE_ONLY, to mark such entries and allows reclaiming their physical slots from the physical reclaim scanner. This change aims to free up physical capacity for new allocations when the swap usage exceeds half of the available space.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v4 08/11] mm, swap: only charge physical swap entries
series_items.patch_summary: This patch modifies the way memory swap is charged to a cgroup's memcg->swap counter. Instead of charging when a vswap entry is allocated, it charges only when the entry acquires physical backing. This change ensures that zswap-backed and zero-filled pages are not counted towards the cgroup's swap usage. The patch also refactors the swap memcg operations into separate helpers for getting, recording, charging, uncharging, and putting the owner, which is a prerequisite for this change. As a result, memory.swap.current will only count on-disk swap usage, allowing cgroups to reclaim their anon memory even with memory.swap.max set to 0 if zswap is enabled.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v4 09/11] mm, swap: add debugfs counters for vswap
series_items.patch_summary: This patch adds two debugfs counters to track virtual swap usage in the Linux kernel. The first counter, 'used', tracks the number of virtual swap slots (pages) currently allocated. The second counter, 'alloc_reject', counts the cumulative number of pages that failed to get a vswap slot. These counters are exposed under the '/sys/kernel/debug/vswap/' directory and provide visibility into virtual swap allocation behavior.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v4 10/11] mm, swap: defer memcg_table allocation for physical swap clusters
series_items.patch_summary: This patch optimizes memory allocation for swap clusters by deferring the allocation of a memcg table until it's actually needed. This is done to reduce unnecessary memory usage in cases where a physical swap cluster only holds vswap backings, which don't require a memcg table. The patch allocates the table eagerly for vswap clusters and for physical clusters when vswap is disabled or not enabled. Otherwise, allocation is deferred until the first direct-use slot is handed out.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v4 11/11] mm, swap: widen swap_info_struct max/pages to unsigned long
series_items.patch_summary: This patch widens the size of swap_info_struct's max and pages fields from unsigned int to unsigned long, allowing the vswap device to exceed its previous 16 TB capacity limit when using 4 KB pages. The new maximum capacity is determined by the cluster_info_pool xarray's allocator limit, which can store up to ~8 PB at a typical SWAPFILE_CLUSTER=512 layout. This change enables larger swap devices and improves system performance for systems with high memory demands.

patches_submitted.patch_summary: This patch series introduces Virtual Swap Space (VSwap), a new feature that allows for efficient and scalable swapping by decoupling swap entries from their backing storage. The current implementation ties swap entries to their backing slot, which can lead to performance issues when swap is used as a cache or when swapoff is frequent. VSwap addresses these issues by introducing a separate data structure for swap entries, allowing for more flexible and efficient management of swap space.

The only issue I saw with that was that zstd is a standalone library that
is imported, so I am not sure how using cpu_feature_enabled() would work
for the maintainers. If the maintainers are happy with it, I think the
below patch is much better.

---

From: Usama Arif <usama.arif@linux.dev>
Date: Thu, 27 Aug 2026 05:34:41 -0700
Subject: [PATCH] zstd: use kernel CPU feature detection on x86

Zstd currently probes CPUID while initializing each compression or
decompression context. This bypasses the x86 feature policy used by the
rest of the kernel and repeats a serializing instruction sequence for
every context.

Use cpu_feature_enabled() in the normal x86 compressor and decompressor
objects. Check ABM, BMI1, and BMI2 because the dispatched functions are
compiled with lzcnt, bmi, and bmi2. The checks are alternatives-patched
at boot.

The effect is especially visible under virtualization, where CPUID
normally causes a VM exit. A 4 KiB crypto_acomp benchmark was run in
one-vCPU KVM guests. Comparing the unpatched baseline with this
three-patch series, the median reported ns/op values were:

                         before    after
  compression            16,777   13,635 ns/op  (-18.7%)
  decompression           3,454    1,006 ns/op  (-70.9%)

Keep the existing raw CPUID fallback for preboot and other builds which
cannot use the normal x86 feature infrastructure. Also retain the early
return when dynamic dispatch is disabled.

Signed-off-by: Usama Arif <usama.arif@linux.dev>
---
 lib/zstd/Makefile               |  5 +++++
 lib/zstd/common/zstd_internal.h | 18 ++++++++++++++----
 2 files changed, 19 insertions(+), 4 deletions(-)

diff --git a/lib/zstd/Makefile b/lib/zstd/Makefile
index be218b5e0ed59..db1d1439f5447 100644
--- a/lib/zstd/Makefile
+++ b/lib/zstd/Makefile
@@ -42,3 +42,8 @@ zstd_common-y := \
 		common/error_private.o \
 		common/fse_decompress.o \
 		common/zstd_common.o \
+
+ifeq ($(CONFIG_X86),y)
+CFLAGS_compress/zstd_compress.o += -DZSTD_USE_KERNEL_CPU_FEATURES
+CFLAGS_decompress/zstd_decompress.o += -DZSTD_USE_KERNEL_CPU_FEATURES
+endif
diff --git a/lib/zstd/common/zstd_internal.h b/lib/zstd/common/zstd_internal.h
index 41f190b533209..f7d3bca650747 100644
--- a/lib/zstd/common/zstd_internal.h
+++ b/lib/zstd/common/zstd_internal.h
@@ -31,6 +31,11 @@
 #include "fse.h"
 #include "huf.h"
 #include <linux/xxhash.h>                /* XXH_reset, update, digest */
+
+/* Use the kernel's CPU feature policy in normal x86 kernel builds. */
+#if defined(ZSTD_USE_KERNEL_CPU_FEATURES)
+#include <asm/cpufeature.h>
+#endif
 #define ZSTD_TRACE 0
 
 /* ---- static assert (debug) --- */
@@ -311,12 +316,17 @@ size_t ZSTD_decodeSeqHeaders(ZSTD_DCtx* dctx, int* nbSeqPtr,
  */
 MEM_STATIC int ZSTD_cpuSupportsBmi2(void)
 {
-#if DYNAMIC_BMI2
-    ZSTD_cpuid_t cpuid = ZSTD_cpuid();
-    return ZSTD_cpuid_bmi1(cpuid) && ZSTD_cpuid_bmi2(cpuid);
-#else
+#if !DYNAMIC_BMI2
     /* Nothing looks at the flag in this configuration. */
     return 0;
+#elif defined(ZSTD_USE_KERNEL_CPU_FEATURES)
+    return cpu_feature_enabled(X86_FEATURE_ABM) &&
+           cpu_feature_enabled(X86_FEATURE_BMI1) &&
+           cpu_feature_enabled(X86_FEATURE_BMI2);
+#else
+    ZSTD_cpuid_t cpuid = ZSTD_cpuid();
+    return ZSTD_cpuid_bmi1(cpuid) &&
+           ZSTD_cpuid_bmi2(cpuid);
 #endif
 }
 
--

series_items.subject: [PATCH v6 11/12] mm: install PMD swap entries on swap-out

mmu_notifier range. Both are guarded by CONFIG_THP_SWAP, since
swap_pmd_cache_lookup() and friends only exist under CONFIG_SWAP and

swap_pmd_cache_lookup(). A PMD swap entry can be moved whole only if
the covered range is empty or backed by one PMD-sized folio. If the

review_comments.summary: Reviewer Luiz Capitulino noted that the set_pmd_swap_entry() function does not check if the PMD size is exact, which can lead to false reporting of success and corruption of MM_ANONPAGES/MM_SWAPENTS accounting. He requested a precondition check for an exact PMD-size folio.

On 2026-08-18 09:09, Usama Arif wrote:
> When reclaim swaps out a PMD-mapped anonymous THP today, the PMD is
> split into HPAGE_PMD_NR PTE-level swap entries via TTU_SPLIT_HUGE_PMD
> before unmap.  This series introduces a PMD-level swap entry so the
> huge mapping can survive the swap round-trip and do_huge_pmd_swap_page()
> can restore the PMD mapping directly on swap-in, without waiting for
> khugepaged to collapse the range later.
> 
> The PMD swap entry is a compact page-table encoding for HPAGE_PMD_NR
> consecutive swap slots.  swap_map accounting remains per-slot and is
> unchanged.  Importantly, a PMD swap entry does not promise that the swap
> cache always contains one PMD-sized folio.  While the cache is empty or
> contains one PMD-sized folio, PMD-level handling can proceed.  Once the
> cache has split/per-slot state, users either inspect the individual
> slots directly (mincore) or split the PMD swap entry and retry through
> the PTE path (fault, swapoff, MADV_WILLNEED, UFFDIO_MOVE).  Likewise,
> if any slot is still backed by zswap's per-page store, PMD-order
> swap-in consumers split and let the PTE path load the range page by page;
> an all-on-disk range can still be read back as one PMD-sized folio.
> 
> The series is ordered so every consumer can handle PMD swap entries
> before the swap-out producer starts installing them.  The swap-out patch
> is the last functional change.
> 
> Notes on zswap:
> 
>    Native PMD-order zswap load/store is intentionally left for a follow-up.
>    Alexandre Ghiti is currently working this.
>    This series can still preserve PMD swap entries while zswap is enabled:
>    zswap stores the THP as order-0 entries, and PMD-order swap-in
>    consumers split any range that has zswap entries before reading it.  If
>    zswap has written the whole range back to disk, or the swap cache still
>    contains one PMD-sized folio, PMD-level handling can proceed.
> 
> Testing:
> 
>    The 16 pmd_swap selftests pass on x86_64 with zswap both disabled and
>    enabled.  PMD_SWAP_DEVICE was set, so the swapoff test ran in both
>    configurations.

I ran the pmd_swap selftests with zswap disabled on x86_64 and arm64, it
worked (noting the fact that on swap-in we may be retrieving the folio
from the swap cache as I commented on the kselftest patch).

review_comments.summary: Confirmed that coherent ZONE_DEVICE folios should be dequeued, but noted that this is a pre-existing issue and requires a separate patch to fix.
review_comments.raw_body:
On Thu Aug 27, 2026 at 12:38 PM EDT, Usama Arif wrote:
> On Wed, 26 Aug 2026 17:20:57 +0100 Kiryl Shutsemau <kirill@shutemov.name> wrote:
>
>> From: "Kiryl Shutsemau (Meta)" <kas@kernel.org>
>> 
>> deferred_split_isolate() probes each queued folio with folio_try_get().
>> folio_try_get() failure is treated as a lost race with folio_put(): clear
>> PG_partially_mapped, correct MTHP_STAT_NR_ANON_PARTIALLY_MAPPED, take
>> the folio off the queue.
>> 
>> The folio_put() race is the most common case for !folio_try_get(), but
>> it is not the only option. Another scenario is folio_ref_freeze().
>> 
>> A zero refcount in such cases does not mean the folio is going away.  It
>> means "don't touch me" and current deferred_split_isolate() doesn't
>> respect it. It can lead to unqueueing folios from the deferred list for
>> no reason:
>> 
>>     CPU 0                            CPU 1
>>     ---------------------------      ------------------------------
>>     freeze a mapped folio            deferred_split_scan()
>>       folio_ref_freeze()               folio_try_get() fails
>>                                        folio_clear_partially_mapped()
>>                                        NR_ANON_PARTIALLY_MAPPED--
>>                                        folio off the queue
>>     give up, put it back
>>       folio_ref_unfreeze()
>> 
>> The folio is still partially mapped, but it is no longer a split candidate.
>> Nothing queues it again until part of it is unmapped once more.
>> 
>> Skip the folio instead: whoever freezes the folio, owns it and owner is
>> responsible for its fate. It also covers the folio_put() case:
>> __folio_put() unqueues the folio via folio_unqueue_deferred_split().
>> 
>> Reported-by: Lance Yang <lance.yang@linux.dev>
>> Link: https://lore.kernel.org/all/20260824131224.73344-1-lance.yang@linux.dev/
>> Assisted-by: Claude-Code:claude-opus-5
>> Signed-off-by: Kiryl Shutsemau (Meta) <kas@kernel.org>
>> ---
>>  mm/huge_memory.c | 19 ++++---------------
>>  1 file changed, 4 insertions(+), 15 deletions(-)
>> 
>> diff --git a/mm/huge_memory.c b/mm/huge_memory.c
>> index ced400f72d43..6281ed993243 100644
>> --- a/mm/huge_memory.c
>> +++ b/mm/huge_memory.c
>> @@ -4590,22 +4590,11 @@ static enum lru_status deferred_split_isolate(struct list_head *item,
>>  	struct folio *folio = container_of(item, struct folio, _deferred_list);
>>  	struct list_head *freeable = cb_arg;
>>  
>> -	if (folio_try_get(folio)) {
>> -		list_lru_isolate_move(lru, item, freeable);
>> -		return LRU_REMOVED;
>> -	}
>> +	/* Lost race to folio_put() or the folio is under folio_ref_freeze() */
>> +	if (!folio_try_get(folio))
>> +		return LRU_SKIP;
>
> I think we might have a problem here for ZONE_DEVICE folios?

For coherent ZONE_DEVICE folios, yes. IIRC, private ZONE_DEVICE folios
are not added to deferred split queue.
>
> This assumes the final put always dequeues the folio, but ZONE_DEVICE folios
> bypass the generic folio_unqueue_deferred_split() path.
> With memcg disabled, this can leave a recycled folio linked on the
> deferred-split list?
>
> Should we dequeue folios in free_zone_device_folio()?

I think so, before mem_cgroup_uncharge().

But it is a pre-existing issue. We need a separate patch unqueuing
folios in free_zone_device_folio() to fix commit a30b48bf1b24
("mm/migrate_device: implement THP migration of zone device pages").

>>  
>> -	/*
>> -	 * We lost race with folio_put(). Read folio state before the
>> -	 * isolate: folio_unqueue_deferred_split() checks list_empty()
>> -	 * locklessly, so once removed the folio can be freed any time.
>> -	 */
>> -	if (folio_test_partially_mapped(folio)) {
>> -		folio_clear_partially_mapped(folio);
>> -		mod_mthp_stat(folio_order(folio),
>> -			      MTHP_STAT_NR_ANON_PARTIALLY_MAPPED, -1);
>> -	}
>> -	list_lru_isolate(lru, item);
>> +	list_lru_isolate_move(lru, item, freeable);
>>  	return LRU_REMOVED;
>>  }

On 27/08/2026 15:25, Lorenzo Stoakes (ARM) wrote:
> On Thu, Aug 27, 2026 at 03:15:47PM +0100, Usama Arif wrote:
>>
>>
>> On 26/08/2026 12:31, Lorenzo Stoakes (ARM) wrote:
>>> Since it's 2026 :) I asked Claude to look at my time as THP co-maintainer:
>>>
>>> 	~107,000 words of review across 948 emails (in 279 distinct
>>> 	threads), counting only prose you actually wrote \u2014 quoted text,
>>> 	signatures and attribution lines stripped. That's a full novel's
>>> 	worth of review commentary.
>>>
>>> 	Along the way you handed out 194 Reviewed-by and 15 Acked-by tags,
>>> 	and your longest single review was 2,404 words (mTHP collapse
>>> 	support, v12 \u2014 the khugepaged/mTHP collapse saga accounts for most
>>> 	of your top-10 longest reviews).
>>>
>>> 	Estimated review time: roughly 300\u2013500 hours, centred around ~400
>>> 	(i.e. ~7 hours/week for 14 months).
>>>
>>> 	1,615 THP-related emails in the window: 948 reviews of others'
>>> 	work, 278 replies on your own THP-touching series threads (~31k
>>> 	more words responding to review), 382 patch emails, and a handful
>>> 	of MAINTAINERS bits. Busiest months: March 2026 (131 review
>>> 	emails), June 2026 (113), August 2026 (111); quietest was December
>>> 	2025 (5).
>>>
>>> Think I can be happy with that!
>>>
>> Ah so sorry to see you step down, you made THP genuinely better!
>>
>> The numbers show the amount of effort you have put in, but they don't capture
>> how consistently useful and detailed your reviews are, with the aim of
>> always trying to make the patches and THP better!
>>
>> Thanks for being an awesome maintainer and hopefully you will consider
>> coming back soon!
> 
> Thanks Usama! :) I know we started off with some fireworks on review \U0001f605 but
> you've always been fantastic to work with and it's been great to see you
> develop as a contributor.
> 
> BTW, I did want to say but never got around to it - I love how you've
> approached the PUD THP stuff - i.e. getting the huge swap stuff sorted
> first, gradually building things up, etc.!
> 
> You've always given interesting sessions + input at LSF and have had great
> insights on how stuff interacts with the Meta fleet also! :)
> 
> It was especially interesting to hear that 512 MiB huge pages have actually
> resulted in far less memory usage than you might expect :)
> 
> I will still be busy upstream with the 4 other maintainerships to keep me
> busy, along with series both in kvmarm and core mm so don't worry I'm not
> going anywhere :)
> 
> And as I said to David and others, always feel free to cc- me or ping me
> off-list etc. if I can be of use for THP stuff, even though I'm taking a
> break from the maintainership side!
> 

Thanks for the kind words! It has been awesome working with you and discussing
different topics at conferences and the mailing list! I am sure we will continue to
in the future!

>>
>> Thanks,
>> Usama
> 
> --
> Cheers, Lorenzo

review_comments.author: Lorenzo Stoakes (ARM)
review_comments.summary: Expressed gratitude for Usama's contributions, highlighting his consistently useful and detailed reviews, and praised his approach to PUD THP.
